newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: FEATURE-Caribbean colonies debate letter from Britain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Caribbean colonies debate letter from Britain.

text.p: Stung by a letter it received from a British Cabinet minister, this tiny colony in the eastern Caribbean is talking of splitting from the mother country, even though that is not what it wants to do.
Though the capital, Plymouth, now sits covered in ash and abandoned, victim of a volcano, independence discussions dominate debates here and in other British Caribbean colonies.

In a Dec. 17 letter, British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind suggested that London might have to extend its power over the Caribbean colonies of Montserrat, Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, Turks and Caicos and the British Virgin Islands to the point of overruling local decisions.
The letter was variously interpreted as a shove toward independence, an ill-advised blunder by Britain and a warning to colonies to toe the line on issues like drug trafficking.

Colombian drug traffickers are increasingly using the islands to ship drugs to the United States, and U.S. and British authorities have pressed Caribbean governments to step up enforcement and crack down on money laundering.

Britain's holdings in the Caribbean, assembled during the days of the British privateers who roamed the Spanish Main in search of plunder, have slowly dwindled in the 20th century as Jamaica, Antigua and Barbuda, St. Kitts and Nevis and others left the fold to make their own way.

In the remaining colonies, tiny and economically frail -- as Montserratians have found out since their volcano came to life in July 1995 and crushed the local economy -- independence talk waxed and waned over the years.

Rifkind's letter said Britain would consider giving its governors, the queen's representatives in the colonies, the power to reject the advice of local elected officials and pass new or amending legislation "if the Legislature refuses to do so and if such legislation is necessary in the interests of public order, public faith or good government."

In Montserrat, where a third of the population has been chased off the island by the active Soufriere Hills volcano and many of the rest depend on the British government for basic necessities, the letter was called "untimely."
"It should not have been sent to us at this time," Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne told Reuters.
A series of public meetings following release of the letter found Montserratians, who flirted with the idea of independence in the past, but have little taste for it now.
"We need to have that support from a larger power," Osborne said. "At the moment, most recognise the advantage of being a dependent territory."

The letter was sent only to Caribbean colonies, which have large black populations, and not to other British territories; Bermuda, the Falkland Islands, St Helena, and Gibraltar. In Anguilla, which receives about $1.6 million in British aid each year, that raised the issue of race.

In Montserrat, ties to Britain are myriad. The Union Jack flies on buildings and the phone book is laced with Meades, Osbornes and O'Garros. It was only a decade ago that then-Chief Minister John Osborne, a cousin of the current chief, railed against classification of the colony as a "dependent territory," insisting that it paid its own way.

Yet now, the volcano-troubled island is virtually dependent on Britain, which has pledged $40 million in aid. Thousands receive weekly food packages from the government and now are well aware of the value of their colonial ties.
"It's younger people who are talking about independence, but the older people have more common sense," said Jim Cartey, a 64-year-old retiree who worked in England as a train conductor for 36 years.

McCartey, who has lived in a church shelter for months after evacuating his home in the volcano danger zone, said Montserrat needs Britain. "We used to grow bananas here. Now we buy them," he said. "The young people think things would be better. But they've got it wrong."

Rifkind's letter pledged that a colonial governor's powers would be extended only if the "conduct of public affairs fall below acceptable standards" and insisted that only the people of the colonies can make a decision on independence.
But some colony leaders remain sceptical.
Hubert Hughes, chief minister of Anguilla, population 10,000, said promises of independence and threats of control are wielded by London as blackmail tactics to keep the colonies in line.
"They come down from the imperial throne at the empire and they want to dominate the economic and political life in the colonies. Anguillans resent that," Hughes said in an interview.
"We are not owned by Britain," he said, adding, "The new power will make a mockery of democracy. A civil servant from the foreign office would be able to ignore the advice of the local council"
